title: Ramadan: the iftar cannon
hook: in some cities a cannon marks sunset for breaking the fast

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fanous, the Ramadan lantern of tin and colored glass. Your line was lanterns for ramadan. Did you light a lamp on purpose last night? Day one thousand forty-two.

Late afternoon in the fasting month. A table is laid: dates in a bowl, water in glasses, soup keeping warm, a plate nobody is allowed to touch yet. Children hover. Somebody checks the window. Somebody else checks a phone. Everyone is listening. Then, from the hill across the city, a deep boom rolls over the rooftops, and the whole house moves at once. A date. A sip of water. Someone laughs. In some cities, that boom is the sound of sunset in Ramadan. Today: the iftar cannon.
screen: `DATES, WATER, AND WAITING.` → `A BOOM FROM THE HILL.` → `THE WHOLE HOUSE MOVES AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: First, what the cannon is answering. The Qur'an sets the edges of the fasting day: eat and drink until the dawn is clear, and then, in Pickthall's translation, "Then strictly observe the fast till nightfall." In Sunni practice the fast ends at sunset, with the call to the sunset prayer; in Shia practice, a little later, when the redness has left the eastern sky. Before clocks on every wrist, a whole city needed to know the same moment at the same time. A call from a minaret carries only so far. A cannon carries much farther. Second, the story. There's a story people tell in Cairo, in several versions: a ruler was testing a new cannon, and by chance it fired just at sunset in Ramadan. The people took it as a signal, and thanked him, and so the firing became a custom. Whether it happened that way, nobody can say. But the custom spread, and in some cities a cannon still fires at sunset in Ramadan, sometimes carried on television and radio. Third, the hurry. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says people will remain in good as long as they hurry to break the fast. Not lingering, not proving how long you can last. When the time comes, eat. The Qur'an gives the fast a firm edge at both ends, and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, asked people not to blur the second one. Fourth, the joy. Another hadith says the one who fasts has two joys: one when breaking the fast, and one on meeting the Lord. The cannon is the sound of the first joy, heard by a whole city at once.
screen: `STRICTLY OBSERVE THE FAST TILL NIGHTFALL.` · `A CANNON FIRED BY CHANCE, THEY SAY.` · `HURRY TO BREAK THE FAST.` · `TWO JOYS FOR THE ONE WHO FASTS.` · then, large: `THE CANNON AT SUNSET.`

segments.voice: The practice: wait for a signal, and then answer it. Settle, and breathe. For the next stretch, simply listen to whatever sounds are around you: traffic, a fridge, a bird, your own breath. Don't do anything with them. Just wait, the way a family waits at the table. When the bell comes, let it be your cannon: take one slow sip of water and notice it. If you're fasting today, you can let this remind you to break the fast on time, without delay. If you pray, you can give thanks in the words you know. The bell holds the time.
Ramadan. The month of fasting from dawn to nightfall, and in some cities, the month a cannon tells everyone at once that the sun is down. Today's word.
Your line: the cannon at sunset. Today, whatever you're waiting for, when it arrives, take it gladly and without delay. Day one thousand forty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims fasting in Ramadan break the fast at the call to the maghrib prayer, at sunset or, in Shia practice, a little after, often with dates and water; in some cities a cannon is fired at that moment.
